std/20.explanation: Tenant restrictions are what stop a user signing in to any tenant other than your own, and in Global Secure Access they are delivered as Universal Tenant Restrictions on the Microsoft traffic profile — that is Microsoft Entra Internet Access. The Global Secure Access feature comparison table lists Universal Tenant Restrictions under the Entra P1/P2 Microsoft traffic profile column only; the Private Access column is blank. Remember the split: Internet Access is the secure web gateway for internet, SaaS and Microsoft traffic, so anything about controlling where users authenticate outbound lives there.
whyWrong: A. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is endpoint detection and response. It does not govern which Entra tenant a user may authenticate to.
C. Microsoft Entra Private Access is the ZTNA half of Global Secure Access, for reaching private on-premises apps. It has no tenant-restriction capability.
D. Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB. It can govern SaaS session behaviour but does not enforce tenant restrictions at authentication.

std/54.explanation: Dangling DNS detection is a named capability of Microsoft Defender for App Service: it alerts when an App Service site is decommissioned and its custom domain (the CNAME) is left behind, which is exactly the subdomain-takeover risk the question describes. The trap here is matching the word 'DNS' in the question to the product with 'DNS' in its name.
whyWrong: A. Defender for DevOps covers the pipeline and repositories, not published DNS records.
C. Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB for SaaS usage.
D. Defender for DNS watches Azure resources for malicious DNS resolution — command-and-control, data exfiltration by DNS — not the lifecycle of a web app's CNAME record.

THIS ANSWER WAS CORRECTED BY AI

Regulatory standards such as NIST SP 800-53 are turned on as security standards in Defender for Cloud — Regulatory compliance > Manage compliance policies > Security policies, then toggle the standard On. Only then does the subscription get assessed and appear on the regulatory compliance dashboard. B. Defender for Cloud Apps access policies govern SaaS sessions and have nothing to do with regulatory assessment.
D. Secure score recommendations measure general posture against the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark, not compliance with a named regulatory standard.

Compare this with Standalone 85, which asks the same thing with 'turn on a security standard' as the wording.

C. The Azure security baseline audit report is a different artefact and is not how a regulatory standard is assessed.

std/92.explanation: B2B direct connect is the one feature built for Teams shared channels, and it satisfies every requirement in the stem: users collaborate with their home credentials so no guest object is created in contoso.com, inbound cross-tenant access settings can be scoped to a group in fabrikam.com, and the trust gives single sign-on. Microsoft's own wording: users 'work together using their home credentials and a shared channel in Teams, without having to be added to each other's organizations as guests.'
whyWrong: A. B2B collaboration invites the external user as a guest object in your tenant — the opposite of the stated requirement — and guests cannot participate in shared channels.
B. Connect Sync synchronises on-premises AD DS to Entra ID; it is not a cross-tenant feature.
C. Cross-tenant synchronisation provisions external users as B2B collaboration users in your tenant, so it also creates the accounts the question forbids.

std/95.explanation: This is the core Global Secure Access split. Microsoft Entra Private Access is the ZTNA service for private, corporate resources — the on-premises App1 — and replaces VPN with per-app access. Microsoft Entra Internet Access is the identity-aware secure web gateway for internet and SaaS destinations, which is what App2 is. Map 'private/on-premises' to Private Access and 'internet/SaaS' to Internet Access and these questions become mechanical.

source.title: What is Global Secure Access?

std/109.explanation: An on-premises FTP server reached from the internet is a private resource on a non-HTTP protocol, and Private Access provides per-app access for TCP and UDP applications with Conditional Access applied per app — that is what makes it ZTNA rather than a VPN. Application proxy would be the older answer but is limited to web apps; Private Access is described as building on application proxy and extending it to any private resource, port and protocol.
whyWrong: B. Microsoft Entra application proxy publishes web applications over HTTP/HTTPS, so it cannot publish FTP.
C. Internet Access secures outbound traffic to internet and SaaS destinations, not inbound access to your own server.
D. Azure Bastion gives RDP/SSH to Azure virtual machines through the portal; Server1 is on-premises and the protocol is FTP.
E. Application Gateway is a regional layer-7 load balancer for HTTP/HTTPS.

std/214.explanation: Legacy applications issuing LDAP queries need a directory that speaks LDAP. Microsoft Entra Domain Services (formerly Azure AD DS) provides managed domain services — domain join, Group Policy, LDAP, and Kerberos/NTLM — without you deploying or patching domain controllers, which is also what satisfies 'minimize the administrative effort'. Microsoft names this exact scenario: cloud-only organisations with third-party apps that still require LDAP.
whyWrong: B. Azure AD B2C is a customer identity service for consumer sign-in.
C. Azure AD (Microsoft Entra ID) is not an LDAP directory — it speaks OIDC, OAuth and SAML.
D. Running AD DS yourself on Azure VMs works but means deploying, patching and monitoring domain controllers, which is the administrative effort the question tells you to minimise.

std/215.explanation:
THIS ANSWER WAS CORRECTED BY AI

This is word-for-word the same scenario as Standalone 214, which the source keys to Azure AD DS — so the source contradicts itself, and the Microsoft Entra ID key here is the wrong half of that contradiction. Microsoft Entra ID does not answer LDAP; it is a modern-protocol identity provider. Microsoft Entra Domain Services is the managed domain that provides LDAP, Kerberos/NTLM, Group Policy and domain join for legacy applications that cannot be modernised.
whyWrong: A. AD DS on your own servers would work but is the maximum administrative effort, which the question rules out.
B. Microsoft Entra ID speaks OIDC, OAuth and SAML. Legacy LDAP binds and reads are not supported against it.
D. Microsoft Entra External ID is for external and customer identities.

source.title: Overview of Microsoft Entra Domain Services

std/280.explanation: An enterprise application that needs LDAP to look up attributes about Entra users needs a managed domain in front of Entra ID. Domain Services synchronises users, groups and credentials one way from Microsoft Entra ID and exposes them over LDAP and Kerberos/NTLM, giving the legacy app what it expects without any domain controllers to run.
whyWrong: A. A Conditional Access trusted location is an access-policy condition and adds no directory protocol.
C. Private Access is network access to private apps; it does not make Entra ID answer LDAP.
D. Pass-through authentication validates passwords against on-premises AD DS during sign-in and is unrelated to LDAP lookups against Entra.

Microsoft Defender for Identity overview

std/24.explanation: Defender for Identity is the only one of these that looks inside an on-premises AD DS domain. Its identity security posture assessments evaluate domain configuration and surface the weaknesses attackers exploit, which is exactly “identify configuration issues and administrative vulnerabilities”, and it does so from a lightweight sensor on the domain controllers rather than a project you have to build — that is the “minimize effort” half.
whyWrong: A. Microsoft Entra ID Protection scores risk on cloud identities (risky sign-ins, leaked credentials). It does not assess AD DS domain configuration.
B. Defender for Servers protects the operating system as a workload, not the directory it belongs to.
D. Microsoft Sentinel is a SIEM. It could ingest the signal, but you would have to write the detections yourself, which is the opposite of minimizing effort.

source.title: Microsoft Defender for Identity overview

std/101.explanation: Credential exposure in an AD DS domain is Defender for Identity's posture territory: it identifies risky configurations and exposures, analyses lateral movement paths showing how an attacker would traverse the environment, and surfaces the findings as remediation recommendations through Microsoft Secure Score. That combination — actionable recommendations, no infrastructure to build — is what the two requirements are testing.
whyWrong: A. Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB for SaaS activity.
B. Secure Score is where some of these recommendations surface, but it is a score, not the product that assesses the domain.
C. The MAP Toolkit is an inventory and migration-planning tool with no security assessment role.

source.title: Microsoft Defender for Identity overview

std/153.explanation: Privilege escalation against a synced on-premises domain is a core Defender for Identity detection: it monitors “privilege escalation and suspicious role or group membership changes” and domain-dominance behaviour such as DCShadow and Golden Ticket. Note the direction of travel — the domain syncs to Entra ID, but the attack happens on-premises, so a cloud identity product cannot see it.
whyWrong: A. Entra ID Protection evaluates cloud sign-in risk, not on-premises privilege escalation.
C. Defender for Servers protects the server workload.
D. PIM governs how Entra roles are activated. It is a preventive control, not a detection for an attack already underway in AD DS.

source.title: Windows LAPS overview

std/27.explanation: Windows LAPS gives every machine a different, automatically rotated local administrator password. Microsoft lists the first benefit as “protection against pass-the-hash and lateral-traversal attacks”, which is the requirement word for word: if one machine's local admin account is compromised, the credential is useless on every other machine, so the ransomware cannot spread sideways with it.
whyWrong: B. Privileged Access Workstations harden the admin’s own device. They do not change the local administrator password on the 500 user machines.
C. PIM does just-in-time elevation for Entra ID roles, not for local Windows accounts.
D. Entra ID Protection detects risky sign-ins and has no role in local account management.

source.title: Windows LAPS overview

std/36.explanation: The question asks what to put in the local Administrators group of a privileged access device, and the keyed answer does not answer that question — configuring LAPS in an emulation mode sets how a password is stored, not who is a member of the group. It is also the wrong direction: Microsoft deprecated the legacy LAPS product as of Windows 11 23H2, and emulation mode exists only to ease migration from an existing legacy deployment. Under least privilege, only Group2 — the team that manages the devices — belongs in the group. The Group1 user who is assigned the device must not be a local administrator on it: that is the whole point of a privileged access device.
whyWrong: B. Legacy Microsoft LAPS is deprecated, emulation mode is a migration aid, and neither configures group membership — which is what the question asks for.
C. Adding the assigned user to the local Administrators group of their own privileged access device breaks least privilege and defeats the purpose of the device tier.

source.title: Endpoint Privilege Management with Microsoft Intune

std/194.explanation: Endpoint Privilege Management lets standard users run specific approved binaries elevated without ever joining the local Administrators group. The detail the question turns on is the elevation type: EPM normally elevates using an isolated virtual account, but its “Elevate as current user” type “runs the elevated process under the signed-in user's own account” — which is precisely the stated requirement that apps run in the context of each signed-in standard user.
whyWrong: B. Windows LAPS manages the local administrator account’s password. Using it means signing in as that separate account, not running as the signed-in user.
C. Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (Entra Permissions Management) governs cloud resource permissions across clouds, not Windows elevation.
D. PIM elevates Entra ID directory roles, not processes on a device.

source.title: Endpoint Privilege Management with Microsoft Intune

std/289.explanation: Installing an application needs administrative rights, and EPM grants exactly that for exactly that binary — elevation is scoped by rules to specific files, logged per elevation, and leaves the user a standard user the rest of the time. Microsoft frames it as supporting Zero Trust by “enabling least privilege access and minimizing lateral movement risks”, which is the phrase the question is pointing at.
whyWrong: A. LAPS would hand Group1 a working local administrator credential — broad standing privilege, the opposite of Zero Trust.
C. PIM covers Entra roles, not application installation on a device.
D. Entitlement management governs access packages for resources, not local elevation.

source.title: Azure Storage firewall rules and network access

std/140.explanation: A network security group cannot protect a storage account at all. NSGs filter traffic at a subnet or network interface inside a virtual network; a storage account is a PaaS service reached through its own public endpoint, which no NSG sits in front of. The control that does this is the storage account firewall: “Each IP network rule enables traffic from a specific public IP address range”, and Microsoft gives the identical example of allowing a client’s public IP. With the firewall configured, only the 20 application servers’ addresses get through and everything else is denied.
whyWrong: A. Service tags are used inside NSG rules, so this fails for the same reason — NSGs do not govern access to a storage account.
B. A Web Application Firewall inspects HTTP for a web application behind Application Gateway or Front Door.
C. Inbound NSG rules govern traffic entering a subnet or NIC, not a storage account.
E. Azure Firewall filters traffic leaving or crossing your network; it is not in the path of an internet client reaching a storage endpoint.

source.title: Lock your Azure resources - considerations before applying locks

std/151.explanation: The requirement that decides this is “minimize the impact on the legacy applications”. A read-only lock blocks the List Keys operation — Microsoft states plainly that “a read-only lock on a storage account prevents users from listing the account keys”, because listKeys is a POST and locks block the control plane. New applications therefore cannot obtain a key, while legacy applications already holding one keep working, since locks do not touch the data plane.
whyWrong: B. Setting AllowSharedKeyAccess to false rejects every request authorized with an account key — it would break the legacy applications outright. Microsoft explicitly says to migrate clients to Microsoft Entra ID before doing this.
C. AllowBlobPublicAccess governs anonymous public read access, a different problem entirely.
D. Rotating keys automatically does not stop anyone from retrieving the current key, and it breaks apps holding the old one.

source.title: Grant limited access to data with shared access signatures (SAS)

std/254.explanation: The keyed answer confuses encryption with access control. Customer-managed keys change which key encrypts data at rest; they grant nobody access and expire for no one. A shared access signature is the delegated-access mechanism, and Microsoft describes it as giving “granular control over how a client can access your data — what resources the client may access, what permissions they have to those resources, how long the SAS is valid”. Scoped to specific blobs, with an expiry, and without making the container public: that is the question restated.
whyWrong: B. Sharing the connection string hands over the account key, granting full access to everything with no expiry.
C. Private Link makes the account reachable privately from a virtual network. External vendors on the internet cannot use it, and it grants no data permissions.
D. Customer-managed keys control encryption at rest. They neither grant nor time-limit access.

std/119.explanation: Flagged as a defective question rather than a wrong key. The stem asks which **two** solutions to include and says each correct answer is a complete solution, but the source records a single letter. Resource-based RBAC in Microsoft Sentinel is what separates the two teams’ log access, and the Azure Monitor agent is what collects the perimeter servers’ event logs — both are needed, and the near-identical Standalone 122 keys exactly that pair. The likeliest explanation is that this copy lost an option or half its key. Answer it as Azure Monitor agent plus resource-based RBAC, and do not treat the graded result here as meaningful.

std/87.explanation: Flagged: the key looks wrong and the source seems to know it. The question asks what forces an upgrade from Microsoft Entra ID Free to Premium; the key says multifactor authentication, but the source’s own explanation links to the Privileged Identity Management documentation, which points at option B instead. That fits the licensing: some MFA is available on the Free tier through security defaults, whereas PIM has always required Entra ID P2. Treat B as the more defensible answer. std/103.explanation: The feature this question is built on no longer exists. Adaptive application controls in Defender for Cloud were deprecated in August 2024, alongside the Log Analytics agent they depended on — Microsoft's retirement table lists the feature with no replacement. The key is left as the source has it because it was right when written, but do not carry this into the exam as a live product: application allowlisting on Windows servers today is App Control for Business, surfaced through Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. The behaviour the stem describes — an allowlist, automatic blocking of anything not on it, and admin approval to promote an app — is what adaptive application controls used to do.
