std/283.explanation: Same retired feature as Standalone 103, and the two are the same question with different option lists. Adaptive application controls in Defender for Cloud were deprecated in August 2024 with no replacement in that product. The key stands as the source recorded it, but the current answer to this scenario is application control in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint — which is exactly what Standalone 275 keys, and why those two apparently contradictory items are both defensible on their own option lists.

source.title: Prepare for retirement of the Log Analytics agent — feature functionality table

std/275.explanation: Application control policies in Defender for Endpoint (App Control for Business, formerly WDAC) enforce an allowlist on the machine: anything not explicitly allowed is blocked until an administrator authorizes it. Note the contrast with Standalone 103 and 283, which key adaptive application controls in Defender for Cloud — the historically expected answer for this exact scenario, but deprecated in August 2024. Defender for Endpoint's application control is the surviving mechanism, and it is the only option here that controls what executes on a server.
whyWrong: A. Conditional Access App Control proxies SaaS sessions through Defender for Cloud Apps. It governs web sessions, not processes on a virtual machine.
B. OAuth app policies govern third-party apps consented into your tenant, not executables on a server.
C. Intune app protection policies protect corporate data inside mobile apps. They do not allowlist software on Windows Server.

std/60.explanation: Flagged: the key looks wrong but the documentation that would settle it has been retired. The requirement is to plant fake cached credentials on client computers. That is the deception capability, whose lures are fake content — documents, configuration files, cached credentials — planted on specific devices, and which is delivered through Defender for Endpoint (option B). A Defender for Identity honeytoken tag does something different: it marks an existing account as a decoy so any authentication to it alerts, and it plants nothing on any endpoint. That distinction is what Standalone 143 tests correctly. Microsoft's deception articles now redirect to the attack-disruption page, so no citable source establishes it and the source's key is left alone.

source.title: Learn about sensitivity labels

std/32.explanation: Watermarks are a content marking, and content markings are a sensitivity label setting in Microsoft Purview Information Protection: a label can “mark the content … by adding watermarks, headers, or footers”. Note the scope detail worth remembering — watermarks apply to documents, not to the body of an email, which is why the question asks about attachments.
whyWrong: A. Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB. It can apply labels to files in third-party services, but it is not what defines the watermark.
B. Insider risk management scores risky user behaviour; it marks nothing.
D. Azure Purview (now the Microsoft Purview Data Map) discovers and catalogues data estates. Content marking belongs to Information Protection.

source.title: Learn about sensitivity labels

std/124.explanation: The phrase that decides this is “regardless of where the data is stored”. Microsoft describes sensitivity labels as protecting content “wherever it's stored”, because the label is written into the file's metadata and the encryption travels with it — across Windows, macOS, iOS and Android, which matches the mixed device estate in the stem. Classification plus encryption in one control is Information Protection.
whyWrong: A. eDiscovery finds and preserves content for legal matters; it neither classifies nor encrypts.
B. Retention policies decide how long content is kept, not who can open it.
C. Compliance Manager scores your posture against regulations. It is an assessment tool, not a protection control.

source.title: Learn about sensitivity labels

std/235.explanation: These two work as a pair, which is why the question asks for two components. Sensitivity labels classify the PII and carry the protection with the file; DLP policies act on that classification to stop it leaving — blocking the share, the upload, or the send. Labels decide what something is; DLP decides what may happen to it.
whyWrong: C. Retention labels govern how long content is kept and what happens at the end of its life, not whether it can be shared.
D. eDiscovery cases search and preserve content for investigations and legal hold. They prevent nothing.

source.title: Learn about sensitivity labels

std/88.explanation: Flagged as genuinely contestable rather than wrong. The source keys sensitivity label policies, and that defends well: a label applies encryption whose usage rights follow the file, so an external recipient cannot open it wherever it ends up. But DLP policies are the control literally designed to prevent sharing outside the organisation, and the near-identical Standalone 235 keys the two together as a pair. Either is defensible as written. On the exam, read for the verb: “classify and protect” points at labels, “prevent from being shared” points at DLP, and where both appear the intended answer is usually both.

source.title: Azure Policy definitions effect basics

std/107.explanation: Flagged, because the effect that actually answers this question is not on the list. To evaluate compliance without changing resources you use the **audit** effect, which reports a resource as non-compliant and does nothing else. The keyed answer, **disabled**, does something different: Microsoft's evaluation order says “disabled is checked first to determine whether the policy rule should be evaluated” — it switches the rule off, so nothing is assessed at all. The likely source of the confusion is that a policy *assignment* also has an enforcement mode whose portal label is **Disabled** (DoNotEnforce), and that one does exactly what the question asks: the policy is evaluated and compliance reported, but the effect is not enforced. Two different settings, one shared word. On the exam, keep effect `disabled` (stop evaluating) apart from enforcement mode `Disabled` (evaluate, don't enforce), and remember `audit` is the effect for reporting without changing anything.
whyWrong: A. Deny blocks the request outright, so it very much changes what happens.
C. Modify alters resource properties, for example adding or changing tags.
D. Append adds fields to a resource during creation, so it also changes resources.

source.title: Configure multi-user authorization using Resource Guard

std/69.explanation: This is the rogue-admin scenario, and multi-user authorization with a Resource Guard is the control built for it. The Resource Guard sits in a different subscription or tenant, and Microsoft requires that the backup admin have no Contributor or Backup MUA Operator rights on it — so a compromised backup admin cannot approve their own destructive action. Deleting backups, disabling soft delete and removing MUA protection are all protected operations, and the last two cannot even be exempted.
whyWrong: A. A security PIN gates critical operations for MARS and MABS agents. It is the on-premises analogue, not the control for a Recovery Services vault in this scenario.
C. Registering MABS with a vault is a setup step; it protects nothing by itself.
D. A PIM role assignment for Backup Contributor grants the destructive permission rather than requiring a second party to approve its use.

source.title: FAQ — Protect backups from ransomware with Azure Backup

std/233.explanation: The question asks which controls ensure you can still restore after an attack, and Microsoft answers it directly under “How to block intentional or unintentional deletion of backup data?” — enable soft delete, and require authorization for critical operations. Soft delete is the one that guarantees restorability: it retains deleted backup data for 14 days, and Microsoft warns that “if backups are deleted and soft delete isn't enabled, you or Microsoft can't recover the deleted backup data.” Requiring a PIN for critical operations is the authorization gate offered here. Azure Monitor notifications are a genuine best practice, but they are detective — being told that backups were disabled does not let you restore from them.
whyWrong: A. Alerting on configuration change tells you an attack happened. It does not preserve a recovery point.
C. Offline copies to Data Box is not an Azure Backup control and is not part of Microsoft’s guidance here.
D. Customer-managed keys change who controls the encryption key. They do nothing to stop a backup being deleted.

source.title: FAQ — Protect backups from ransomware with Azure Backup

std/195.explanation: For workloads protected by the MARS agent or Azure Backup Server, the security PIN is the authorization gate on critical operations — disabling backup, deleting backup data, changing a passphrase — so a compromised administrator on the server cannot quietly stop protection before encrypting the estate. That is what “increase the resiliency of the backup strategy” means here: keep the recovery points reachable.
whyWrong: A. Geo-redundant storage protects against a regional outage, not against someone deleting the backups.
B. Customer-managed keys change key ownership; they neither prevent deletion nor preserve recovery points.
D. Site Recovery replicates workloads for disaster recovery. Replication faithfully copies encrypted data too, so it is not a ransomware control.

source.title: What's Microsoft Entra Permissions Management? (archived — retired 1 November 2025)

std/96.explanation: The product this question keys no longer exists. Microsoft Entra Permissions Management stopped being available for purchase on 1 April 2025 and was retired on 1 November 2025; its documentation is archived. The key was right when written — Permissions Management was the CIEM tool giving “cross-cloud permissions discovery… for AWS, Azure, and GCP” — so it stands, but do not carry it to the exam as a live answer. Multicloud permission visibility now comes through Defender for Cloud's CIEM capabilities in Defender CSPM.

source.title: What's Microsoft Entra Permissions Management? (archived — retired 1 November 2025)

std/262.explanation: Same retired product as Standalone 96. Permissions Management was the tool that measured the gap between permissions granted and permissions used, and could automatically delete permissions unused for the past 90 days — which is why the key matched the stem so exactly. It was retired on 1 November 2025 and its documentation is archived, so treat the underlying idea (find unused entitlements, right-size them) as the examinable point rather than the product name.

source.title: What's Microsoft Entra Permissions Management? (archived — retired 1 November 2025)

std/288.explanation: Access reviews in Privileged Identity Management are the surviving answer. PIM covers Azure resource roles as well as directory roles, so it can enumerate who holds privileged assignments across subscriptions and drive a recurring review of whether they still need them. Note the distractor: option A names the Permissions Management analytics dashboard, which would have been a reasonable answer historically but was retired on 1 November 2025 — so on the current exam this pair is no longer a close call.
whyWrong: A. Microsoft Entra Permissions Management was retired on 1 November 2025.
B. Access reviews in ID Governance cover group and application access; privileged role assignments are reviewed through PIM.
D. Defender EASM discovers your internet-facing attack surface. It has nothing to do with role assignments.

source.title: Overview of Azure Policy

std/113.explanation: Azure Policy evaluates resources whenever one is created or updated in a scope with an assignment, and again on a compliance cycle every 24 hours — so a newly deployed non-compliant resource is detected automatically. ISO 27001 ships as a built-in initiative, which is a group of policy definitions assigned together. Note the pairing with Standalone 258: same standard, and Azure Policy is the answer to both, because it is the engine that does the evaluating whichever product surfaces the result.
whyWrong: A. Azure Blueprints is deprecated and packaged artefacts for deployment rather than evaluating ongoing compliance.
B. The regulatory compliance dashboard in Defender for Cloud is where results are read. The evaluation underneath it is Azure Policy, and the question asks what to use to enforce.
C. Azure RBAC governs who may act, not whether the resulting resource is compliant.

source.title: Overview of Azure Policy

std/258.explanation: The word that decides this is “remediated”. Azure Policy “helps to bring your resources to compliance through bulk remediation for existing resources and automatic remediation for new resources”, using the deployIfNotExists and modify effects with a remediation task. No other option here changes a resource at all.
whyWrong: A. The regulatory compliance dashboard reports compliance; it remediates nothing on its own.
C. Azure Blueprints is deprecated and deploys artefacts rather than remediating drift.
D. Azure RBAC controls permissions, not resource configuration.

source.title: Overview of Azure Policy

std/137.explanation: Restricting which regions resources may be created in is the textbook Azure Policy case — Microsoft lists “Ensure your team deploys Azure resources only to allowed regions” as a headline governance action, and ships a built-in **Allowed Locations** definition with a Deny effect “used to enforce your geo-compliance requirements”.
whyWrong: A. Regulatory compliance standards in Defender for Cloud assess against published frameworks; they do not enforce a company-specific region rule.
B. A custom Azure role decides who can create a resource, not where it may live.
D. Management groups are the scope you assign a policy to, not the mechanism that enforces anything.

source.title: Overview of Azure Policy

std/242.explanation: Every recommendation in the list — restrict network access, use virtual network rules, require a private link, disallow public access — is a resource configuration, and Azure Policy is the service that evaluates and enforces resource configuration at scale. Each of these has a built-in definition, and assigning them stops the drift returning rather than just reporting it again next week.
whyWrong: A. Storage Analytics is metrics and logging for a storage account.
B. Network Watcher diagnoses network connectivity and traffic.
C. Sentinel is a SIEM: it would alert on the misconfiguration, not prevent it.

source.title: Overview of Azure Policy

std/163.explanation: The Microsoft cloud security benchmark is delivered as an Azure Policy initiative, so keeping deployed App Service apps compliant with it means assigning that initiative and letting Azure Policy evaluate each app as it is created or updated. The distractors are all about the pipeline rather than the deployed resource.
whyWrong: A. DevOps security in Defender for Cloud assesses the repositories and pipelines, not the running App Service.
B. Defender for App Service detects threats against the running app; it does not enforce a benchmark.
C. A branch policy gates code review before merge, well before anything is deployed.

source.title: Enable vulnerability scanning with Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management

std/250.explanation: The product in the key is still right; the requirement in the stem is not. Defender for Servers does provide vulnerability assessment, but it no longer uses the Qualys engine — “Defender for Cloud uses Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management to scan your machines”, in agentless and agent-based modes, and the Qualys-based solution has been retired. A question that asks you to pick a product *because it uses Qualys* can no longer be answered as written. Remember the current pairing: Defender for Servers is the plan, Defender Vulnerability Management is the scanner inside it.

source.title: Enable vulnerability scanning with Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management

std/187.explanation: Hardware and firmware assessment is a premium Defender Vulnerability Management capability, not part of the vulnerability scanning included with Defender for Servers Plan 1. Adding the Defender Vulnerability Management add-on is what turns it on for servers already covered by Plan 1 — which is also why upgrading the plan is not the minimal answer.
whyWrong: A. Moving every server to Plan 2 is a far larger change and is not what gates firmware assessment.
C. Azure Update Manager reports and installs operating system updates; drivers and firmware are not its job.
D. The Intune Suite add-on extends endpoint management features, not server vulnerability assessment.

source.title: Protect folders from ransomware with controlled folder access

std/176.explanation: Controlled folder access exists for exactly this: “Ransomware encrypts your files and holds them hostage. CFA counters this threat by allowing only trusted apps to change files in protected folders.” It is an attack surface reduction capability in Defender for Endpoint, delivered by Microsoft Defender Antivirus, and it protects the user profile folders by default.
whyWrong: B. Azure Files is cloud file storage, not a control on the endpoint.
C. Device Guard (now App Control for Business) controls which code may run, a different control from guarding a folder’s contents.
D. Defender for Endpoint is the platform that contains the feature. The question asks which control to use, and CFA is the specific one.
E. BitLocker encrypts the volume at rest. It does not stop a process running on the signed-in device from encrypting files.

source.title: Protect folders from ransomware with controlled folder access

std/130.explanation: “Protected folders” names the controlled folder access element that does the work — Microsoft defines them as “the folders that CFA guards. Untrusted apps can't modify or delete files in these folders.” This is the same question as Standalone 176 with the option worded differently, and the same reasoning picks it out: the specific control beats the platform it lives in.
whyWrong: A. Defender for Endpoint is the platform; the question asks for the control.
B. Device Guard restricts which code can execute.
D. Azure Files is storage, not an endpoint control.
E. BitLocker protects data if the device is lost or stolen; it is transparent to a process running as the signed-in user.

source.title: Automate threat response with playbooks in Microsoft Sentinel

std/40.explanation: Playbooks are Sentinel's SOAR component: automated workflows, built on Logic Apps, that run against an alert or incident. Both requirements land on them. “Respond to threats right away with minimal human involvement” is the response use case, and Microsoft's orchestration example is exactly the Teams requirement — “send a message to your security operations channel in Microsoft Teams or Slack so your security analysts know about the incident.”
whyWrong: A. Data connectors bring data in. They are the SIEM plumbing, not the automated response.
C. Workbooks visualise data in dashboards; they take no action.
D. KQL is the query language the detections are written in, not an automation mechanism.

source.title: Web content filtering in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

std/83.explanation: Web content filtering in Defender for Endpoint “enables your organization to track and regulate access to websites based on their content categories”, and the question names the categories almost verbatim: **Adult content** is a parent category and **Gambling** one of its children. Blocks are enforced by SmartScreen in Edge and by network protection in other browsers, on-premises or away from the network.
whyWrong: A. Endpoint Manager (Intune) deploys the policy in some designs but is not the filtering capability itself, and the categories live in Defender.
B. Compliance Manager scores regulatory posture.
C. Defender for Cloud Apps governs SaaS app usage and can block unsanctioned apps, but category-based web filtering on the device is a Defender for Endpoint web protection feature.

source.title: Create session policies in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps

std/171.explanation: This needs both halves and the question says so. A Defender for Cloud Apps **session policy** with Conditional Access App Control is what inspects the live session and blocks the download — Microsoft's own example is allowing access from unmanaged devices while limiting the download of sensitive files. But a session policy cannot work alone: “in order for your session policy to work, you must also have a Microsoft Entra ID Conditional Access policy”, which routes the session through Defender for Cloud Apps in the first place.
whyWrong: B. Application Proxy publishes on-premises web apps; SharePoint Online is already a cloud service.
C. Azure Data Catalog is a data discovery service, long superseded, and unrelated.
E. Purview Information Protection can label and encrypt the file, but it does not block the download action based on device management state.

source.title: Create session policies in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps

std/278.explanation: Defender for Cloud Apps is Microsoft's CASB and the MCRA component for SaaS visibility and control. Its session policies “provide granular visibility into cloud apps with real-time, session-level monitoring”, which is the “in real time” part of the requirement, and its activity policies and anomaly detections cover risky behaviour across connected apps.
whyWrong: A. Purview Information Protection classifies and protects content; it does not monitor user activity across apps.
C. Defender for Endpoint sees the device, not the SaaS session.
D. Sentinel could ingest and correlate the signal, but it is the SIEM downstream. The question asks which service provides the visibility, and for SaaS that is Defender for Cloud Apps.

source.title: Security baselines assessment in Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management

std/172.explanation: Security baselines assessment is the Defender Vulnerability Management feature built for exactly this: it “helps you to continuously and effortlessly monitor your organization's security baselines compliance and identify changes in real time”, comparing devices against a base benchmark — and CIS benchmarks for Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server are explicitly supported. Devices configured to CIS at deployment and later modified show up as non-compliant against the profile.
whyWrong: A. An authenticated scan reaches unmanaged devices; these devices are already onboarded.
B. Microsoft Secure Score for Devices is an aggregate posture score, not a per-device CIS compliance result.
C. Attack surface reduction rules harden the device against specific attack techniques; they do not measure benchmark drift.

source.title: Ingest syslog and CEF messages to Microsoft Sentinel with the Azure Monitor Agent

std/64.explanation: There is no direct path from an arbitrary firewall into Sentinel, so you put a collector in between. Microsoft's documented pattern is a Linux machine running a syslog daemon (rsyslog or syslog-ng) that the appliances forward CEF messages to; the Azure Monitor Agent on that machine parses them and sends them to the workspace as CommonSecurityLog. The absence of a built-in connector for this particular firewall is exactly why the generic CEF-over-Syslog path exists.
whyWrong: A. A logic app automates a response to an incident. It is not a log ingestion path for on-premises appliances.
C. The on-premises data gateway bridges Power BI, Logic Apps and Power Automate to on-premises data sources. It does not collect syslog.
D. Data Factory moves data for analytics pipelines, not security event streams into a SIEM.

source.title: Visualize and monitor your data by using workbooks in Microsoft Sentinel

std/127.explanation: Workbooks are Sentinel's visualisation layer: interactive reports and dashboards built from workspace data, with a library of built-in templates and full support for custom views. The words in the stem, custom views and a dashboard for analysing events, map onto workbooks and nothing else here.
whyWrong: A. Playbooks automate a response. Compare Standalone 40, where the requirement is action rather than analysis.
C. Notebooks host Jupyter-based hunting and data science investigations, not an operational dashboard.
D. Threat intelligence brings in indicators of compromise; it is a data source, not a view.

source.title: Log Analytics workspace data export in Azure Monitor

std/165.explanation: The direction of travel decides this. Data connectors bring data into Sentinel; getting data out to a third-party SIEM goes the other way, and the supported mechanism is a Log Analytics workspace data export rule with an event hub as the destination. Splunk then reads from the event hub using the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Cloud Services. Event Hubs is the standard hand-off point between Azure Monitor and any external consumer.
whyWrong: B. Data Factory is an ETL and data movement service for analytics workloads, not a streaming egress for security events.
C. A workbook renders data inside Sentinel. It exports nothing.
D. A data connector is inbound. This is the trap in the question: it is the right noun pointing the wrong way.

source.title: What is Microsoft Sentinel?

std/170.explanation: Read the four requirements together: centrally manage incidents, analyse logs, audit activity, and hunt, all across every deployed service. That is a SIEM, and Sentinel is the only option that spans both the Azure subscription and the Microsoft 365 estate. The cost requirement is about not standing up several overlapping tools, not about picking the cheapest product in the list.
whyWrong: A. Microsoft 365 Defender (now Defender XDR) correlates across the Microsoft 365 workloads, but does not cover the Azure subscription resources.
B. Defender for Cloud is CSPM and cloud workload protection for Azure resources; it is not where you audit Microsoft 365 activity.
C. Defender for Cloud Apps covers SaaS usage only.

source.title: View MITRE ATT&CK coverage in Microsoft Sentinel

std/183.explanation: Sentinel's MITRE ATT&CK page presents the framework as a matrix and shades each technique by how many active detections you have for it, which makes the gaps the visible thing on the screen. That is what the question is asking for: not a list of your rules, but the techniques your rules do not cover. Because the matrix is refreshed as Sentinel tracks new framework versions, it also keeps answering the question as ATT&CK evolves.
whyWrong: A. The Health Summary dashboard reports connector and rule health, not detection coverage.
B. There is no Sentinel feature by the name MITRE analytics explorer.
D. The Analytics blade lists the rules you have. It tells you what is covered, not what is missing.

source.title: Threat intelligence report in Microsoft Defender for Cloud

std/290.explanation: Flagged: half of this key is well supported and half is not. Threat intelligence reports in Defender for Cloud (option B) are exactly what the stem describes. Microsoft's page says they help you learn more about the threat that triggered an alert and give incident response teams information about the detected threat, including how to remediate it. No Microsoft source, however, establishes that Sentinel threat intelligence workbooks (option D) supply remediation guidance for an alert; a threat intelligence workbook visualises indicators of compromise. Option A, workload protections in Defender for Cloud, arguably has a better claim, since the alert detail there carries remediation steps. Because the question says each correct answer is a complete solution, and only one of the keyed pair can be defended from documentation, the key is left as the source has it and the item is flagged rather than guessed at.

source.title: Get started using Attack simulation training

std/108.explanation: Note the verb: identify which users are susceptible, not block the phishing. Attack simulation training in Defender for Office 365 runs benign simulated phishing campaigns against your own mailboxes and reports who clicked, who entered credentials and who reported the message, which is how you measure susceptibility and then assign training to the people who need it.
whyWrong: A. Spoof intelligence tells you which external senders are spoofing your domain. That is about the senders, not about your users.
B. Attack path analysis models exploitable paths through Azure resources; it has nothing to do with mailboxes.
D. Insider risk management scores risky behaviour by your own users, which is a different risk from being taken in by an attacker.

source.title: What is entitlement management?

std/115.explanation: All three requirements are entitlement management features, and entitlement management is part of Microsoft Entra ID Governance. An access package for App1 gives users a self-service request through the My Access portal; the request policy can attach requestor questions, which is the extra information demanded at request time; and an access review on the assignments, run every three months with the manager as reviewer, is the recurring attestation.
whyWrong: A. Application Proxy publishes on-premises web applications. App1 is already SaaS and already integrated.
B. Connected apps in Defender for Cloud Apps give you visibility and control over a SaaS app, not a request and approval lifecycle.
D. Access policies in Defender for Cloud Apps allow or block a session; they do not govern who is entitled to the app.

source.title: Delegation and roles in entitlement management

std/211.explanation: The second requirement is what decides this, and it is easy to read past. Keeping an access package out of My Access is the Hidden setting: set to Yes, the access package is not listed in the user's My Access portal. Microsoft's delegation table maps both requirements onto roles precisely. Directly assign and directly remove an identity are permitted to the Access package assignment manager, but Hide an access package is not; that row is granted only to the Identity Governance Administrator, the Catalog owner and the Access package manager. So the assignment manager satisfies the first bullet and fails the second. The least privileged role that satisfies both is Access package manager, which Microsoft describes as able to create new access packages from existing resources in the catalog, and edit and manage all existing access packages within the catalog.
whyWrong: A. Identity Governance Administrator can do all of this, but tenant-wide across every catalog, which is more privilege than a department team leader needs.
B. Catalog owner also covers both actions, but adds the ability to add and remove resources and to delegate the catalog itself. Still more than required.
C. Access package assignment manager is the tempting least-privilege answer and covers the first bullet only. It cannot change the Hidden setting.

source.title: Get started with content explorer

std/223.explanation: The requirement is to identify documents that contain sensitive information, and content explorer is the tool that answers it. Microsoft describes it as showing a current snapshot of the items that have a sensitivity label, a retention label, or are classified as a sensitive information type in your organization, and you can drill into Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams locations, which is the exact scope in the stem. DLP is a preventive control: it acts when someone tries to share or move content that matches a sensitive information type. It protects, it does not inventory. Read the verb in these questions. Identify or discover points at content explorer and the data classification pages; prevent, block or restrict points at DLP.
whyWrong: B. DLP enforces policy on sensitive content in motion. It is the answer when the requirement is to stop something, as in Standalone 224.
C. eDiscovery searches and preserves content for a legal matter or investigation. It is case-driven, not a standing inventory of sensitive data.
D. Information governance (now data lifecycle management) is about retention and disposal, not classification discovery.

source.title: Learn about Endpoint data loss prevention

std/224.explanation: The action to be blocked, uploading a file to a website, happens in a browser on the device, so the policy has to reach the device. That is the Devices location, which is endpoint DLP. Its Upload to a restricted cloud service domain or access from an unallowed browser activity works from a list of service domains: allow the Microsoft OneDrive domains and block the rest, and you get exactly the pair of requirements in the stem. Applying the policy to the SharePoint location would govern the file while it sits in SharePoint, which is not where the leak happens.
whyWrong: B. The OneDrive accounts location governs content in OneDrive itself; it does not control uploads to third-party sites.
C. The SharePoint sites location governs sharing from SharePoint. Once the file is on the endpoint, that policy no longer applies.
D. Defender for Cloud Apps can block uploads to unsanctioned cloud apps through a session policy, but the question asks which DLP location to use, and browser upload control is the Devices location.

source.title: Use Intune to remediate vulnerabilities found by Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

std/236.explanation: Security tasks is the node that carries Defender Vulnerability Management findings into Intune. Microsoft's instruction is literally the question: Sign in to the Microsoft Intune admin center, select Endpoint security > Security tasks, choose a security task to view its details. A security task states the type of vulnerability, priority, status and steps for remediation, and one of the two remediation types is Configuration, for example configuring a setting in the Microsoft Defender Antivirus profile. That is the recommended configuration change the stem asks about, and the Intune admin accepts or rejects it there.
whyWrong: A. Device compliance evaluates devices against your own compliance policy and drives Conditional Access. It does not surface vulnerability findings.
B. Endpoint detection and response policy onboards devices to Defender for Endpoint and tunes EDR. It is a configuration you author, not a list of recommendations you review.

C. Attack surface reduction is the node where you author ASR, controlled folder access and exploit protection policies. Hardening settings you deploy, not recommendations coming back from Defender Vulnerability Management.

source.title: GitOps with Flux v2 in Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes and AKS

std/42.explanation: Declarative configuration held in a repository and continuously reconciled onto clusters is the definition of GitOps, and in Azure the GitOps agent is Flux v2, deployed as a cluster extension on AKS and Arc-enabled Kubernetes. The Flux controllers pull the manifests from the repository and keep the cluster matching them, which is what keeps twenty clusters consistent without anyone applying anything by hand.
whyWrong: A. Gatekeeper (used by Azure Policy for Kubernetes) admits or rejects resources against policy. It enforces rules about configuration; it does not deliver the configuration.
B and C. Dependency Tracker and Dependency are not the mechanism here; dependency scanning is about vulnerable packages in code.

source.title: Always Encrypted with secure enclaves

std/51.explanation: Work through the requirements and only one option survives. Pattern matching on encrypted columns server-side needs Always Encrypted with secure enclaves, which rules out plain Always Encrypted. Of the two enclave technologies, Intel SGX is the hardware-based one and is the type used by Azure SQL Database with attestation through Microsoft Azure Attestation; VBS enclaves are virtualization-based, that is, software. Hardware-based encryption plus Azure Attestation therefore points at SGX. The enclave is also what keeps the DBA and privileged malware out: the plaintext only ever exists inside it.
whyWrong: A. SQL Server on Azure VMs with VBS enclaves is IaaS and the enclave is software-based, failing the hardware requirement.
B. Azure SQL Database with VBS enclaves meets most requirements but again is not hardware-based.
C. Azure SQL Managed Instance with Always Encrypted but no enclave cannot do the server-side pattern matching.

source.title: Entity tags in Microsoft Defender for Identity

std/72.explanation: Both halves of the requirement are one Defender for Identity feature. The Sensitive entity tag supports users, devices and groups, and Microsoft notes that some detections, like sensitive group changes, rely on this tag. Tag Group1 as sensitive and any modification to it raises a Defender for Identity alert, which reaches Sentinel through the connector with no rule to write. That is what minimises administrative effort. Worth remembering: Defender for Identity marks a fixed list of groups (Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Backup Operators and so on) sensitive automatically, but Exchange Organization Management is not on it, so this one has to be tagged by hand.
whyWrong: A. ID Protection scores risky sign-ins and users. It says nothing about group membership changes in AD DS.
C. Defender for Office 365 protects mail and collaboration content, not directory objects.
D. PIM governs eligibility and activation for Entra roles and Azure resources. Group1 is an on-premises AD DS group in an Exchange role group, which is outside its scope.

source.title: Dynamic data masking in Azure SQL Database

std/123.explanation: Minimise patching effort and minimise cost together push you to the most managed, least expensive option that still supports the feature, and dynamic data masking is available in Azure SQL Database. Being a PaaS database, Microsoft handles the patching entirely, and a single database is cheaper than Managed Instance or a VM.
whyWrong: A. Managed Instance also removes patching but costs considerably more; it is the answer when you need instance-scoped features such as SQL Agent or cross-database queries.
B. Synapse dedicated SQL pools are for data warehousing, and are neither the cheapest nor the natural landing place for a migrated OLTP database.
D. SQL Server on Azure VMs leaves the operating system and SQL patching with you, which is exactly what the stem asks you to avoid.

source.title: Develop secure applications on Azure

std/125.explanation: The vulnerability list in the stem is copied almost word for word from Microsoft's definition of dynamic application security testing: DAST tools analyse programs while they are executing, to find security vulnerabilities such as memory corruption, insecure server configuration, cross-site scripting, user privilege issues, SQL injection, and other critical security concerns. Insecure server configuration in particular can only be seen at runtime, which is what settles it against SAST.
whyWrong: A. IAST instruments the running application from the inside. It is a real technique, but Microsoft frames this exact vulnerability list as the DAST case.
B. SAST analyses source code or compiled code when it is not executing, so it cannot see how the deployed server is configured.
C. RASP defends the application at runtime; it is a protective control, not a test.

source.title: Authorize access to blobs using Microsoft Entra ID

std/136.explanation: Blob containers and Data Lake Storage Gen2 are the same service (Gen2 is Blob storage with a hierarchical namespace), and both authorize requests with an OAuth 2.0 token issued by Microsoft Entra ID, so Entra security applies directly to data operations. Disk Storage has no such data-plane identity model at all; a managed disk is reached through the VM. Worth knowing where the line has moved: Azure Files does now support identity-based access, but it works differently. Azure Files uses the Kerberos protocol to authenticate with an identity source, whether on-premises AD DS, Entra Domain Services or Entra Kerberos, rather than presenting an Entra OAuth token the way blob does. The examinable pair is still blob and Data Lake Storage Gen2; treat Azure Files as the case to think twice about.
whyWrong: A. Azure Disk Storage is attached to a virtual machine and has no identity-based data-plane authentication.
C. Azure Files supports identity-based authentication over SMB, but through Kerberos tickets from a domain source, not direct Entra ID token authorization.

source.title: Entity tags in Microsoft Defender for Identity

std/143.explanation: Microsoft's description of the honeytoken tag is the requirement restated: tag honeytoken accounts to set traps for malicious actors, these accounts are usually dormant, and any sign-in from a honeytoken account triggers an alert. Because the accounts have no legitimate use, any authentication at all is suspicious, which makes them a very low false-positive detection. Contrast Standalone 60, which asks for fake credentials planted on client computers: that is deception in Defender for Endpoint, and a honeytoken plants nothing on an endpoint.
whyWrong: A. Standalone sensors are a deployment option for the sensor software, not a detection feature.
C. Sensitivity labels are a Purview classification control for content.
D. Custom user tags let you group entities for filtering and reporting. Only the Honeytoken tag creates the alerting trap.

source.title: Rapidly modernize your security infrastructure (privileged access RaMP)

std/149.explanation: Microsoft opens the RaMP article with its purpose: this rapid modernization plan will help you quickly adopt Microsoft's recommended privileged access strategy. It is a prioritised roadmap of initiatives, separate privileged accounts, turn on PIM, require phishing-resistant MFA for admins, block legacy authentication, deploy privileged access workstations, and it is the Zero Trust guidance for privileged identity specifically.
whyWrong: A. ESAE, the red forest, is the legacy on-premises hardened forest model. Microsoft has retired it in favour of the modern privileged access strategy.
B. The Security Development Lifecycle governs how software is built.
D. Operational Security Assurance is about how Microsoft runs its own services, not a customer design framework for privileged identity.

source.title: Malware scanning in Microsoft Defender for Storage

std/166.explanation: Malware scanning in Defender for Storage is triggered on upload: a blob written to a container is scanned in near real time and the result is surfaced as a scan result and an alert, which is precisely detect threats in files after the files are uploaded. It is an add-on capability of the Defender for Storage plan, enabled per storage account.
whyWrong: A and B. Both Defender for Containers capabilities protect Kubernetes and container images, not a blob container. The word container in the stem is storage terminology and this is the trap.
D. Sensitive data threat detection tells you the blob holds sensitive data and raises the severity of alerts about it. It is about the sensitivity of the content, not about the file being malicious.

source.title: Azure Monitor Logs reference: CDBDataPlaneRequests

std/181.explanation: Auditing who touched the data needs two things: every request must be attributable to an identity, and every request must be recorded. Disabling local authentication is the first half. While the account keys work, any caller holding a key is indistinguishable from any other, so no log can name a user. Sending the Cosmos DB diagnostic logs to a Log Analytics workspace is the second half. The DataPlaneRequests category captures every data plane operation for the Cosmos DB account, and its table carries AadPrincipalId, the AAD Principal ID of the caller issuing the data plane request, alongside the operation, the container and the client IP. Entra sign-in logs were the keyed choice but they record token issuance, not the individual reads and writes against a container, so they cannot show which users accessed the data.
whyWrong: A. Defender for Cosmos DB detects anomalous and potentially malicious access. It is threat detection, not an audit trail of all access.
B. Entra sign-in logs show authentication events, not per-request data plane activity against the account.
D. Defender for Identity monitors Active Directory and identity infrastructure. It has no view of Cosmos DB.

source.title: What is Conditional Access in Microsoft Entra ID?

std/234.explanation: Zero Trust has three principles, and each maps onto a control: verify explicitly, use least privilege access, assume breach. Conditional Access is the enforcement point for verify explicitly. It is the policy engine that takes the signals gathered at sign-in, user, device, location, application, risk, and decides whether to grant access, block it, or require another factor. In the MCRA, Conditional Access sits in front of resources as exactly that gate.
whyWrong: A. Defender for Cloud gives you posture and workload protection. It is an assume-breach control rather than the verification gate.
C. Identity Governance handles entitlements and reviews, which serves least privilege, not explicit verification at access time.
D. Defender for Identity detects attacks against identity infrastructure. Detection, not verification.

source.title: Web Application Firewall DRS rule groups and rules (Azure Front Door)

std/249.explanation: Three requirements, and only one service satisfies all three. Front Door is a global service that routes each user to the nearest healthy backend, which Application Gateway, being regional, cannot do for apps spread across regions. The WAF policy attached to Front Door uses the Default Rule Set, which is based on the OWASP Core Rule Set. And Front Door issues and renews Microsoft-managed TLS certificates for custom domains, which is where minimise administrative effort is decided.
whyWrong: A and C. Azure Firewall, in either tier, is a network firewall. Even Premium with IDPS is not an OWASP CRS web application firewall.

D. Application Gateway with WAF does the OWASP inspection well, but it is regional, so meeting the routing requirement would mean one per region plus something in front of them. That is more administrative effort, not less.

source.title: What is Zero Trust?

std/265.explanation: Both keyed controls are the Zero Trust principles applied directly. Blocking sign-ins from unknown locations is verify explicitly, using location as a signal in the access decision. Blocking sign-ins from non-compliant devices is device health as a condition of access, which is the same principle plus assume breach. The two distractors are useful precisely because they are the pre-Zero-Trust habits the model rejects.
whyWrong: B. Always allowing connections from the on-premises network is the network perimeter assumption that Zero Trust exists to replace. Location does not confer trust.
C. Disabling passwordless sign-in for sensitive accounts moves in the wrong direction. Zero Trust calls for stronger, phishing-resistant authentication on privileged accounts, not weaker.

source.title: Encryption scopes for Blob storage

std/286.explanation: The mechanism here is an encryption scope, and Microsoft states its two levels plainly: encryption scopes enable you to manage encryption with a key that is scoped to a container or an individual blob. The question asks for the most granular level, and the individual blob, which in a Data Lake Storage Gen2 account is a file, is more granular than the container. A scope set on a container is only the default for blobs uploaded into it, and unless the container prohibits overrides, an individual blob can be uploaded with a different scope. Encryption scopes are fully supported on accounts with a hierarchical namespace, so the Data Lake Gen2 detail in the stem does not push the answer back up to the container.
whyWrong: A. The account level is where the default key applies. It is the least granular option, not the most.
B. A folder is a hierarchical namespace construct. It is not an encryption boundary; encryption scopes know about containers and blobs.
D. The container is the keyed answer and is a real level, but it is the default for the blobs inside it rather than the finest one available.

source.title: Secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud (security controls table)

std/4.explanation: No, and the reason is worth learning because it settles all three questions in this family. Secure score is organised into controls, and a recommendation only moves the control it belongs to. Microsoft describes Secure management ports, worth 8 points, as recommendations that "reduce your exposure with tools like just-in-time VM access and network security groups". Adaptive network hardening belongs to a different control: Restrict unauthorized network access, worth 4 points, which Microsoft describes as where you "manage adaptive network hardening in Defender for Cloud". Enabling it improves that control, not this one. To move Secure management ports, close the management ports, put the VMs behind NSGs, and turn on just-in-time VM access.

source.title: Just-in-time machine access in Microsoft Defender for Cloud

std/61.explanation: No. The VMAccess extension is an operations tool: it resets a local administrator password, resets the SSH key or configuration, and can add a user to a VM that has become unreachable. It opens nothing, closes nothing, and appears in no recommendation under Secure management ports. The recommendations in that control are about closing management ports, protecting internet-facing VMs with network security groups, and gating RDP and SSH with just-in-time access, which opens the port only for an approved user, from an approved source IP, for a limited time.

source.title: Secure score in Microsoft Defender for Cloud (security controls table)

std/106.explanation: No. Onboarding machines to Defender for Endpoint is a real improvement, but it lands in the Enable endpoint protection control, worth 2 points, which Microsoft describes as checking "your organization's endpoints for active threat detection and response solutions" and recommending you deploy Defender for Endpoint if none is present. Secure management ports is a network exposure control. EDR detects an attacker who has already reached the machine; it does not reduce the brute-force surface that the control measures.

source.title: Network conditions in Conditional Access policy (named locations, countries)

std/7.explanation: Blocking by country is a Conditional Access named location. You define a countries-and-regions named location, then write a policy that targets the enterprise applications and blocks access when the sign-in comes from that location. Standalone 12 is the identical question with the options reordered, so recognise the pattern rather than the letter.
whyWrong: A. Activity policies in Defender for Cloud Apps act on activity in a session after access is granted, and only for connected apps.
B and E. Risk policies in ID Protection respond to a calculated risk level, not to a list of countries you choose.
C. Device compliance policies decide whether a device meets your standard; they say nothing about where the user is.

source.title: Network conditions in Conditional Access policy (named locations, countries)

std/12.explanation: The same question as Standalone 7 with a different option order, and the same answer: a Conditional Access policy using a countries and regions named location. Watch the letters on these paired items. Reading the option text rather than remembering "the answer was D" is what protects you when the exam shuffles them.
whyWrong: B and E. ID Protection risk policies react to risk signals, not to a chosen list of countries.
C. Activity policies in Defender for Cloud Apps govern in-session activity, not the initial connection.
D. Intune device compliance policies evaluate the device, not the location.

source.title: Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage encryption

std/9.explanation: Yes, and it is the rotation requirement that makes customer-managed keys necessary rather than merely acceptable. All Azure Storage data is encrypted with 256-bit AES whichever key type you choose, so the AES-256 requirement is satisfied either way. What Microsoft-managed keys will not give you is control of the schedule: with a customer-managed key in Key Vault you own the key lifecycle and can rotate it monthly, manually or on an automated rotation policy, and Azure Storage can be set to pick up the new version automatically.

source.title: Encryption scopes for Blob storage

std/74.explanation: No, and this is the companion to Standalone 9. An encryption scope is a real feature and it can indeed be protected by either a Microsoft-managed key or a customer-managed key, so the mechanism in the stem exists. The problem is the key type. Microsoft manages the rotation of its own keys on its own schedule, and you cannot drive it. Only the customer-managed key option lets you choose to "update the key version either automatically or manually", which is what a monthly rotation requirement demands.

source.title: Govern discovered apps using Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

std/47.explanation: Yes. Cloud Discovery is the half of Defender for Cloud Apps that scores apps, ranking more than 31,000 catalogued cloud apps against roughly 90 risk factors, which is where "Microsoft has identified as high risk" comes from. A cloud discovery policy can flag apps by risk score, and tagging an app Unsanctioned is what enforces the block: with the Defender for Endpoint integration turned on, network protection stops users on those devices from reaching unsanctioned apps, while apps left sanctioned or untagged stay reachable. Discovery supplies the risk score, the tag supplies the decision, and Defender for Endpoint supplies the enforcement.

source.title: SaaS Security Posture Management (SSPM) in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps

std/55.explanation: No. SSPM answers a different question from the one in the stem. It "offers detailed visibility into the security state of your software as a service (SaaS) applications" by assessing their configuration against benchmarks, and Microsoft states the precondition plainly: those recommendations appear only "after you connect the SaaS application by using an app connector". So SSPM looks at apps you have already adopted and wired up, tells you their settings are weak, and recommends fixes. It does not enumerate the shadow-IT apps users have found for themselves, it does not carry Microsoft's catalogue risk score, and it blocks nothing. Access policies are also the wrong lever: they run through Conditional Access App Control, which you configure per app for apps you sanction, not as a sweep against every high-risk app on the internet. The solution that does meet the goal is the one in Standalone 47.
whyWrong: A. Yes is not defensible: SSPM assesses connected apps and produces recommendations, and neither half of the stated requirement, identifying high-risk apps or blocking them, is something it does.

source.title: Govern discovered apps using Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

std/63.explanation: No, and it is a close-looking miss. Web content filtering in Defender for Endpoint does block sites on managed devices, but it decides what to block by content category (adult content, gambling, and so on), which is what Standalone 83 tests. The requirement here is to allow or block by Microsoft's risk assessment of the app, and there is no category called "high risk". The mechanism that does read the risk score is unsanctioning an app in Defender for Cloud Apps, which then blocks it through the same Defender for Endpoint network protection plumbing. Same enforcement engine, different decision input.
whyWrong: A. Yes would require a category-based policy to know Microsoft’s app risk score, and it does not.

source.title: Govern discovered apps using Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

std/142.explanation: No. Neither piece of this solution knows anything about app risk scores. Intune app protection policies are data-protection policies applied inside managed apps: they stop copy and paste to personal apps, require a PIN, and can wipe corporate data. Conditional Access can block access to a cloud app, but only to apps you name in the policy, one at a time, and it has no view of the Defender for Cloud Apps catalogue. Blocking by Microsoft's risk assessment across thousands of apps needs Cloud Discovery and the Unsanctioned tag.
whyWrong: A. Yes would require these two controls to act on Microsoft’s risk rating of SaaS apps. Neither has access to it.

source.title: Set up Azure App Service access restrictions

std/80.explanation: No, because virtual network integration governs the wrong direction. It gives the app outbound access into a virtual network so it can reach private resources such as a database or a storage account behind a private endpoint. It does not filter who may call the app. Restricting inbound callers to Front Door is what access restrictions are for, which is the subject of Standalone 97 and 129.
whyWrong: A. Yes confuses outbound integration with inbound access control. The app’s public endpoint stays open to the internet.

source.title: Set up Azure App Service access restrictions

std/97.explanation: No, and the reason is practical rather than conceptual. Filtering by IP address is a legitimate technique, but Front Door does not call your origin from one stable backend address. It is a globally distributed service whose egress addresses change as the platform scales, so a rule pinned to today's address is a future outage. That is exactly why Azure publishes the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag, which resolves to the whole current set and is maintained for you. Standalone 129 is the version of this question that uses it.
whyWrong: A. Yes would require Front Door to have a fixed backend IP address, which it does not.

source.title: Set up Azure App Service access restrictions

std/129.explanation: Yes. An access restriction rule built on the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag allows the app to accept traffic only from Front Door's backend address ranges, and Azure keeps the tag current as those ranges change, so nothing breaks when the platform scales. One refinement is worth carrying into the exam: a service tag admits any Front Door instance, not only yours, so Microsoft's own guidance pairs the rule with a check on the X-Azure-FDID header carrying your Front Door ID. The keyed answer is the mechanism the question is testing; the header is what pins it to your instance.

source.title: Getting started with the Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool

std/56.explanation: The Threat Modeling Tool works from a data flow diagram, and Microsoft's walkthrough says so in as many words: a user drawn as an outside entity, a web server as a process, a database as two parallel lines, and then "what Ricardo just showed Cristina is a DFD, short for Data Flow Diagram". The tool adds trust boundaries as red dotted lines and generates threats from where data crosses them, using STRIDE. Data flows and trust boundaries are what produce threats, which is why this diagram type and no other.
whyWrong: B, C and D. System flow, process flow and network flow diagrams are not what the tool builds. Its stencils, its trust boundaries and its STRIDE analysis are all defined in terms of data flow diagram elements.

source.title: Set up secret scanning for GitHub Advanced Security

std/76.explanation: GitHub Advanced Security is the bundle that adds code scanning and secret scanning to repositories, and secret scanning is the capability that finds credentials committed into source. The stem says the source is in Git repositories and the pipeline is Azure DevOps, which GitHub Advanced Security covers in both homes: GitHub Enterprise for GitHub-hosted repositories, and GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps for Azure Repos.
whyWrong: A. Defender for Key Vault detects unusual access to a vault at runtime. It never sees your code.

C. DevOps security in Defender for Cloud gives security teams a single view of findings across pipelines, but the scanning itself is done by GitHub Advanced Security. The question asks what to implement to do the scanning.
D. Dev Box provisions developer workstations.

source.title: What is Microsoft Entra application proxy?

std/89.explanation: The VPN is the attack surface the question wants removed. Application Proxy publishes an internal web app through Microsoft Entra ID without opening any inbound port: a lightweight connector inside the network makes an outbound connection to the service, and every request is authenticated by Entra ID first, so Conditional Access, MFA and device state all apply before a packet reaches Server1 or Server2. That is explicit verification in front of the app rather than network-level trust behind a tunnel, which is the MCRA Zero Trust position.
whyWrong: A. Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB for SaaS sessions, not a publishing mechanism for on-premises web apps.
B. Web protection in Defender for Endpoint governs which sites the device may reach outbound. It does not secure inbound access to your apps.
D. Adding Entra authentication to the VPN improves the tunnel but keeps the tunnel, and with it broad network access. Zero Trust wants access to the application, not to the network.

source.title: Regulatory compliance standards in Microsoft Defender for Cloud

std/91.explanation: The regulatory compliance dashboard in Defender for Cloud is the service that assesses Azure resources against published frameworks, and NIST is among the standards you can add to a subscription alongside the Microsoft cloud security benchmark that is applied by default. The assessments underneath are Azure Policy definitions, which is why Defender for Cloud can report a per-control pass or fail for your actual resources.
whyWrong: A. Compliance Manager scores your Microsoft 365 and organisational posture, largely through assessments you complete. It is not the tool that evaluates Azure resource configuration.
C. Sentinel is a SIEM. Compliance posture is not what it measures.
D. Defender for Cloud Apps assesses SaaS apps, not Azure resources.

source.title: Security admin rules in Azure Virtual Network Manager

std/112.explanation: The problem is not that a rule is missing but that owners can add their own, so the fix has to sit above network security groups. Security admin rules in Azure Virtual Network Manager do exactly that: they are evaluated before NSG rules and a Deny there cannot be overridden by an NSG, so a subscription owner who adds an allow rule for RDP from the internet no longer gets one. Deny inbound 3389 from the internet at the network manager and the only remaining path to the VMs is bastion1.
whyWrong: A. Connectivity configurations build the topology, mesh or hub and spoke. They do not filter traffic.
C and D. Azure Firewall rules only apply to traffic routed through the firewall. Direct RDP that an NSG permits never reaches it, so neither rule type closes the bypass.

source.title: Automated investigation and response in Microsoft Defender XDR

std/10.explanation: Read the requirement literally: minimise the operational load on Tier 1 analysts. Microsoft's page on automated investigation and response answers it by name. "Imagine having a virtual analyst in your Tier 1 or Tier 2 security operations team. The virtual analyst mimics the ideal steps that security operations would take to investigate and remediate threats", working continuously and taking on "a significant load of investigations and threat remediation", which frees the team for other work. AIR, marketed as self-healing, triages the alert, reaches a verdict on each piece of evidence and applies remediation such as quarantining a file or isolating a device. Triage of routine alerts is precisely what Tier 1 does, which is why this and not a governance control is the answer.
whyWrong: A. Built-in compliance policies in Azure Policy improve resource governance. They generate posture findings rather than removing analyst work, and they do not touch the SOC queue.
C. Automating data classification helps protect data and enriches investigations, but it does not triage alerts.
D. Hunting queries are proactive work done by Tier 3 hunters. They add work at the top of the SOC rather than removing it at the bottom.

source.title: Management groups - Cloud Adoption Framework

std/17.explanation: The archetype management groups beneath Landing zones are Corp and Online, and what separates them is connectivity. Microsoft defines Corp as "for workloads that require connectivity or hybrid connectivity with the corporate network via the hub in the connectivity subscription", and Online as "for workloads that might require direct internet inbound or outbound connectivity or for workloads that might not require a virtual network". The guidance states the principle generally too: create management groups under the landing zone management group "based on the security, compliance, connectivity, and feature needs of the workloads". What makes this correction firm is that the same article rules out all three distractors explicitly.
whyWrong: A. “Don’t create management groups for production, testing, and development environments.” Separate those into different subscriptions in the same management group instead.
B. “Use management groups for policy assignment versus billing and RBAC purposes.” Chargeback structure is the wrong axis.
D. “Don’t create management groups solely to model different Azure regions.” Geography is only a factor where data residency or sovereignty law forces it.

source.title: Learn about Microsoft Entra Private Access

std/78.explanation: Server1 is on-premises, and that is what decides it. Microsoft Entra Private Access is the Global Secure Access capability built for this: you specify "the fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) and IP addresses that you consider private or internal", a private network connector inside your network brokers the connection outbound, and "remote workers don't need to use a VPN to access these resources if they have the Global Secure Access Client installed". Because the resource is published as an enterprise application, you assign User1 and apply a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA, which is the second half of the requirement. RDP is just a port and an IP address to Private Access. One honest caveat: Azure Bastion's IP-based connection can reach a machine outside the virtual network, but only one your Bastion virtual network can already route to over ExpressRoute or a site-to-site VPN. The stem offers no such link and says the connection is over the internet, so Bastion would need infrastructure the question does not give you.
whyWrong: A. Entra Internet Access secures outbound traffic to internet and SaaS destinations. It is the other half of Global Secure Access and points the wrong way.
B. Windows Admin Center is a management console. It does not publish RDP to the internet or enforce MFA.
C. Azure Bastion is a service you deploy into an Azure virtual network to reach machines it can route to. It is not a remote access gateway for an on-premises server reached over the internet.

source.title: Encryption and key management in Azure - Cloud Adoption Framework

std/81.explanation: The question asks what belongs in every landing zone, platform and application alike, and Cloud Adoption Framework answers it for key vaults directly: "Don't use centralized instances of Key Vault for application keys or secrets", and "to avoid secret sharing across environments, don't share Key Vault instances between applications." Microsoft gives the reasons: multiple vaults reduce the blast radius of a compromise, avoid throttling from noisy neighbours, and align key management to application boundaries. The other three options are all platform resources. The landing zone architecture puts them in the connectivity subscription, which "hosts the Azure networking resources, like Azure Virtual WAN, Azure Firewall, and Azure DNS private zones, that the platform requires" - deployed once and shared, not repeated per landing zone.
whyWrong: A. Private DNS zones are centralised in the connectivity subscription so that name resolution is consistent across the estate.
C. Azure Firewall is a shared platform service in the connectivity subscription. One per landing zone would be expensive and would fragment egress policy.
D. Virtual network gateways are hub resources in the connectivity subscription.

source.title: Microsoft cloud security benchmark - DevOps Security

std/104.explanation: The risk named in the stem is the third-party and open-source components, and Dependabot is the control aimed at it. The Microsoft cloud security benchmark's DevOps security guidance says to "use Dependabot to ensure that the vulnerable dependency is tracked and remediated" and to keep the repository up to date with the latest releases of the packages it depends on. Dependabot alerts fire when a new advisory affects something in your dependency graph, and the ecosystems it covers line up with the three languages in the stem: Maven for Java, NuGet for C#, pip for Python. Secret scanning is a genuine GitHub Advanced Security capability, but it finds credentials committed into your own code, which is a different failure. That is what Standalone 76 tests.
whyWrong: A. NuGet Audit covers .NET packages only, so it leaves the Python and Java components unwatched.
B. Secret scanning finds exposed credentials in the repository. Valuable, but not the compromised-dependency risk the stem describes.
D. App governance in Defender for Cloud Apps governs OAuth apps consented into your Microsoft 365 tenant. It has no view of your build dependencies.

source.title: Take response actions on a device in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

std/145.explanation: This is a post-breach plan for computers that are already compromised, so the answer has to be a containment action, and in Defender for Endpoint that is device isolation. Microsoft's description matches the ransomware case exactly: "Depending on the severity of the attack and the sensitivity of the device, you might want to isolate the device from the network. Device isolation can help prevent the attacker from controlling the compromised device and performing further activities such as data exfiltration and lateral movement." The isolated device stays connected to the Defender service so investigation continues while the attacker's path is cut. The keyed answer, application isolation, is not a Defender for Endpoint response action at all; the nearest real feature, Application Guard, is a pre-breach hardening control.
whyWrong: A. Controlled folder access is preventive. It stops untrusted apps writing to protected folders before an attack succeeds, which is what Standalone 176 and 130 test.
B. Application isolation is not a response action in Defender for Endpoint. Application Guard hardens browsing and documents in advance.
C. Memory scanning is a detection technique, not a containment step.
E. There is no user isolation action. The identity-side equivalents are disabling the account or forcing a sign-out, which are separate controls.

std/147.explanation: Flagged for a defect in the source rather than a dispute about the answer. In the published exam dump the option list for this question is broken: what should be four options appears as three, because option D ran into option C on the page and was extracted as the single string "Microsoft Sentinel D. Compliance Manager connectors". The intended fourth option, Compliance Manager connectors, is very likely the answer, since it is the mechanism that brings assessment data from AWS and GCP into Compliance Manager, monitors it continuously and supplies improvement actions with implementation guidance. But because the option cannot be selected on its own, the item is not answerable as printed and the key is left untouched. This is the only merged-option defect in the whole bank; the remaining 309 questions parse cleanly.
